title: the Samkhya Karika)
hook: a bed doesn't sleep in itself: how the Samkhya Karika argues for a witness it can't point to

segments.voice: Yesterday we named everything in Samkhya's count, the twenty-four principles: senses, mind, elements and the rest, with purusha outside the list. Where did your ordinary moment land? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.
screen: `THE WHOLE COUNT, NAMED.` · `A BED FOR SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: A bed doesn't sleep in itself. Somebody built a frame, stretched the slats, laid the mattress, smoothed the sheet, folded the blanket at the foot. Every part was fitted to every other part. And the whole thing is plainly for someone who isn't part of the bed. Nobody looks at a made bed and thinks it was arranged for the benefit of the pillow. That's an ordinary thought, and the Samkhya Karika builds an argument on it. From today we read the Karika itself, and we start with its question: how can anyone know the witness is there at all?
screen: `A BED DOESN'T SLEEP IN ITSELF.` → `ARRANGED FOR SOMEONE.` → `HOW DO WE KNOW THE WITNESS?`

segments.voice: First, the book. Near its end, the Samkhya Karika tells its own family tree. The teaching came from the sage Kapila, who passed it to Asuri, who passed it to Panchashikha, and through a line of students it reached Ishvarakrishna, who set it down in these verses. Now the problem. Purusha never acts. It doesn't think, decide or move. So how could anyone know it's there? The Karika answers in one verse with a short string of reasons, and the first is the bed. Whatever is put together, it says, exists for the sake of another. Commentators make it concrete with exactly that picture: a bed, made of parts, for a sleeper who isn't one of the parts. Now look at a body. Bones, breath, senses, a mind, a sense of I, all fitted together. Samkhya asks: for whom? Not for the parts. For someone outside the assembly. The verse adds more. There has to be something beyond the three gunas. There has to be one the whole thing is overseen for, and one who experiences it. And people strive for release, which makes no sense unless someone is there to be released. Notice what kind of argument this is. Samkhya can't point at purusha. It infers it, the way you'd infer a sleeper from a carefully made bed. You may find the argument convincing or not; other schools weigh it differently. But it's an honest move: reasoning from ordinary things to what can't be seen.
screen: `KAPILA TO ISHVARAKRISHNA.` · `PURUSHA NEVER ACTS. HOW DO WE KNOW?` · `WHAT'S PUT TOGETHER IS FOR ANOTHER.` · `INFERRED, NOT POINTED AT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel the bed being made. Sit, and let your breath settle. Notice the arrangement you are right now: the spine holding you up, the lungs filling, the heart keeping time, the ears taking in the room. All of it fitted together, all of it working. Don't analyze. Just let the whole assembly be felt at once. Then rest in the simple fact that it's all being experienced, and leave the one experiencing it unnamed. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the body that's been made. The bell holds the time.
The Samkhya Karika. Ishvarakrishna's verses on Samkhya, which reason that whatever is put together, like a bed, is for someone outside it: purusha.

Your line: the Samkhya Karika. Today, when you make a bed, set a table or pack a bag, notice it's arranged for someone, and ask who the arrangement of you is for. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: The Samkhya Karika is read verse by verse with classical commentaries such as Gaudapada's, and its arguments, like the one for purusha, are studied alongside the replies of other schools.

notes: Index title, word and carry read 'the Samkhya Karika)' with a stray parenthesis from the outline parse ('Samkhya (the 24 principles; the Samkhya Karika)'). Kept exactly; spoken voice drops the parenthesis. Suggest fixing the outline.
Day 1171 already covered Karika 1–3 (suffering, remedies, the count), so this first 'Samkhya Karika' day takes Karika 17 instead.

Karika 17 paraphrase: purusha exists because aggregates are for another's sake; because there must be something other than the three gunas; because there must be a controller (adhishthana); because there must be an enjoyer/experiencer; and because of activity toward release (kaivalya). The bed (shayana) example is from the commentaries (e.g. Gaudapada, Vachaspati). Confirm.
Lineage (Kapila, Asuri, Panchashikha, then a succession to Ishvarakrishna) paraphrased from Karika 70–71; confirm verse numbers. No date given for Ishvarakrishna by design.

'You may find the argument convincing or not' is meant as open, not as telling the listener what they think; 'other schools weigh it differently' points to Buddhist and other critiques without naming or ranking them.
